## Glossary {#glossary}

The four terms below follow the definitions in @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms. They are not interchangeable, and the course depends on the difference: a finding can survive every robustness check on its own data and still fail on new data, or survive the checks and still be one that nobody can recompute from the original materials. The column 'In this course' notes where each idea appears in the four cases.

| Term | Definition | In this course |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| **Reproducibility** | Same question · same data · same analysis → same result | Tested across the SCORE sample by @MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial. In the EU-frames case, the result reported by the original author (OA) was not reproducible from the original materials; in the immigration-and-trust case, the OA supplied no data or code, and two reproductions from the ESS files came close to the published coefficient without matching its sample; in the housing-audit case, SCORE never attempted a reproduction, and the SCORE dossier of the cohabitation case holds none. In every case the class reproduces in Task 3 a value that Multi100 recorded for one of the analysts |
| **Robustness** | Same question · same data · justifiable alternative analysis → stable result | The Multi100 design [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]; the five analysts of each claim; the specification menu and the curve of the claim in Tasks 4 and 5, with 64 specifications in the housing-audit case, 192 in the immigration-and-trust case, 144 in the cohabitation case and 864 in the EU-frames case |
| **Replicability** | Same question · independent new data → same result | Tested across the SCORE sample by @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial. For the housing-audit claim, a preregistered audit of 3,050 housing authorities found no significant gap; for the immigration-and-trust claim, two replications on later rounds of the ESS found the same positive and significant association; for the cohabitation claim, a replication on later NSFG surveys, which tested an interaction of education and period rather than the coefficient that Multi100 used, did not replicate it; for the EU-frames claim, a replication on later Eurobarometer waves was judged not successful |
| **Repeatability** | Umbrella term covering all three above | Used in the glossary of Nosek and colleagues as the overarching category |

## The cases

Each case has a case study that tells its story in full, and the records below are the public deposits on which those pages are built.

### The housing-audit case

**The paper.** The paper of the original authors (OAs) [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect], published in the *American Journal of Political Science*: <https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12252>. The accepted manuscript is open at OpenBU, <https://hdl.handle.net/2144/37826>, and the page numbers quoted on the course site refer to it.

**The data.** The replication package of the OAs on the Harvard Dataverse, released under CC0: <https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU>. It holds the blinded data file, two Stata do-files (one that runs the analyses on the public file, and one written for the identifiable data, which are not public), two codebooks and a ReadMe that explains why the community variables are given in thirds. The course data in `cases/housing/data/` are built from it, and the codebooks beside them describe every column.

**SCORE and Multi100 on the OSF.** The SCORE project of the paper on the Open Science Framework holds every activity that SCORE carried out on it, and the Multi100 component holds one sub-component for each of the five analysts. Four of the five published their scripts there; the course links to them and does not copy them.

| Component | What it holds | Address |
|---|---|---|
| SCORE project of the paper | The parent of the components below | <https://osf.io/3a8bg/> |
| Original materials | The materials of the original study collected by SCORE | <https://osf.io/nrt4s/> |
| Reproduction | A reproduction with the data and code of the OAs, which holds only an unfilled template | <https://osf.io/9wp8d/> |
| Power analysis | The power analysis for the replication | <https://osf.io/kcsby/> |
| Replication | The replication with new data, with its preregistration and final report | <https://osf.io/2ug8x/> |
| Replication data | The de-identified data of the replication, its analysis do-file and a dictionary, in the folder "Public Data"; the licence is unstated, so the course links to them and does not copy them | <https://osf.io/xseqg/> |
| Multi100 | The five reanalyses of the claim | <https://osf.io/38rsh/> |
| 8PTRZ | Chi-square test of a two-by-two table, Hispanic against all other names | <https://osf.io/j8wvh/> |
| UYV3F | Logit without covariates, Hispanic against white names (a review document only) | <https://osf.io/3672s/> |
| EWFMI | Logit of three groups with covariates, in Stata | <https://osf.io/jhvca/> |
| 25N5D | Two-proportion test on every delivered email to Hispanic and white names | <https://osf.io/v8zah/> |
| P9W8Y | Three-group logit with an omnibus test | <https://osf.io/pzwbm/> |
| The Multi100 project | The project as a whole, with the claims of all hundred studies | <https://osf.io/q5h2c/> |

The three activities of SCORE ended in three different places on the same paper. The reproduction was never attempted. The five reanalyses agreed on the direction of the gap and split three to two on whether the data supported the claim, and the replication with new names and a wider set of authorities found no significant gap. The [case study](cases/housing/index.qmd) tells the story in full.

### The immigration-and-trust case

**The paper.** The paper of the original author (OA) [@McLaren2012CulturalDivideEurope], published in *World Politics*: <https://doi.org/10.1017/S0043887112000032>. Its web appendix, which lists the far-right parties of each country and their shares of the vote, is held by the University of Nottingham (eprints.nottingham.ac.uk/1566), with a copy in the SCORE dossier.

**The data.** The European Social Survey, rounds 1–4, from the ESS Data Portal (<https://ess.sikt.no/>), licensed by ESS ERIC under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The course extract `cases/trust/data/trust_ess.csv` is adapted from those rounds and carries the same licence; its [codebook](cases/trust/data/trust_ess_codebook.md) lists the editions read and every change made to them. The country variables come from the appendix of the paper, the World Bank and Eurostat ([codebook](cases/trust/data/trust_macro_codebook.md)).

**SCORE and Multi100 on the OSF.** The paper went through two reproductions from the ESS files, because the OA supplied no data or code, and through two replications on later rounds. The analysis file of the second reproduction is the file that Multi100 gave the five analysts; it states no licence, so the workspace downloads it when Task 3 runs rather than shipping it.

| Component | What it holds | Address |
|---|---|---|
| SCORE project of the paper | The parent of the components below | <https://osf.io/3ajr9/> |
| Original materials | A list of files | <https://osf.io/k6ymx/> |
| Power analysis | The power analysis for the replications | <https://osf.io/j9ge2/> |
| Reproduction | A reproduction from the ESS files, with its report and code; the web appendix of the paper is in its sub-component <https://osf.io/j5fhy/> | <https://osf.io/jp7tr/> |
| Reproduction and replication | A second reproduction from the ESS files, whose analysis file the five analysts received, and a replication on rounds 5–9 | <https://osf.io/e48gd/> |
| Replication | A replication on round 5 | <https://osf.io/rpumq/> |
| Reproduction with author data | A reproduction "with author data & code", which holds only the list of claims | <https://osf.io/j9mpv/> |
| Multi100 | The five reanalyses of the claim | <https://osf.io/9jvbt/> |
| N8P2J | The model of Table 3 of the paper on distrust of parliament | <https://osf.io/npavt/> |
| FQ1G7 | Trust in parliament with a random intercept for each country and eleven controls, in jamovi | <https://osf.io/q8r57/> |
| LT39B | A single immigration item, with country dummies and random intercepts, in Stata | <https://osf.io/y465m/> |
| 456AD | The index over the answered items, with shorter controls, in Stata | <https://osf.io/e7pbq/> |
| 6U3LL | The model of Table 3 without unemployment, the result that Task 3 reproduces | <https://osf.io/s7t9d/> |

The reproductions came close to the published coefficient of 0.17 without matching the sample of the paper, the five reanalyses all found the association that the paper reports, and both replications found it again on later rounds. The [case study](cases/trust/index.qmd) tells the story in full, including how the rebuild of the course and the SCORE reproduction coded the vote controls differently.

### The cohabitation case

**The paper.** The paper of the original authors (OAs) [@KuoRaley2016DivergingPatternsUnion], published in *Demography*: <https://doi.org/10.1007/s13524-016-0483-9>. The author manuscript is open in PubMed Central (PMC5026877).

**The data.** The public-use files of the National Survey of Family Growth (NSFG), released by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) at <https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/Datasets/NSFG/>. They are in the public domain, and their use is bound by the NCHS data use restrictions: statistical reporting and analysis only, and no attempt to identify a respondent. The course rebuilds the first premarital cohabitations of five cycles into `cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_unions.csv` ([codebook](cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_unions_codebook.md)) and turns them into person-months ([codebook](cases/cohabitation/data/cohab_months_codebook.md)).

**SCORE and Multi100 on the OSF.** The OAs supplied no data or code, the dossier holds no reproduction, and the replication team built a person-month file from the NSFG that the five analysts then received. That file is public, and the course ships it as `cases/cohabitation/data/score_person_months.csv` ([codebook](cases/cohabitation/data/score_person_months_codebook.md)).

| Component | What it holds | Address |
|---|---|---|
| SCORE project of the paper | The parent of the components below | <https://osf.io/kv38j/> |
| Original materials | Three empty components | <https://osf.io/q27ua/> |
| Power analysis | No public files | <https://osf.io/gzu2r/> |
| Replication | The replication on secondary data, with its report | <https://osf.io/u8x9s/> |
| Replication files | The person-month file (<https://osf.io/b6p3j/>), its data dictionary and the script | <https://osf.io/jkzdq/> |
| Audit of the replication | The audit of the replication | <https://osf.io/zcy2e/> |
| Multi100 | The five reanalyses of the claim | <https://osf.io/b69nv/> |
| 73FDT | A multinomial logit on the five surveys, then a regression of the five marriage coefficients on the year | <https://osf.io/k7zq2/> |
| N8ZYW | A logit of marriage on the later survey, in jamovi | <https://osf.io/dymz4/> |
| 456AP | A multinomial logit on the person-months of 2002 and 2013–2015 | <https://osf.io/2m38h/> |
| 5X3KG | A test of two proportions on the rows of 1995 and 2006–2010, the result that Task 3 reproduces | <https://osf.io/q6skv/> |
| JDA15 | A logit of marriage on the five surveys with years since 1995 | <https://osf.io/uxgzp/> |

The five reanalyses split two to one to two on the claim, largely because of what the person-month file holds for 1995, and the replication on later surveys, which tested an interaction of education and period, did not replicate it. The [case study](cases/cohabitation/index.qmd) tells the story in full; read it after Task 3 if you follow the one-day or the semester track, because it gives away what the task asks you to find.

### The EU-frames case

**The paper.** @Teney2016DoesEUEconomic – Teney (2016). Does the EU economic crisis undermine subjective Europeanization? *European Sociological Review*, 32(5), 619–633. <https://doi.org/10.1093/esr/jcw008>

**Data and project links.**

| Resource | URL |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Multi100 – OSF project | <https://osf.io/q5h2c/> |
| Multi100 – GitHub repo (effect sizes) | <https://github.com/marton-balazs-kovacs/multi100> |
| OSF fork – data & maintained analysis (course fetch target) | <https://osf.io/6zqct/> |
| Official Multi100 archival record for analyst C6HJR | <https://osf.io/8rtwe/> |
| Full SCORE dossier on the EU-frames case | <https://osf.io/h7432/> |
| Multi100 navigation sheet (claims list) | Available from the Multi100 OSF project above |

#### The SCORE dossier on the EU-frames case {#the-eu-frames-case-score-dossier-one-paper-all-three-rs}

The target article [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic] was put through all three SCORE activities: reproduction, robustness reanalysis, and replication. Few papers have been, which is why this one case can serve for a whole day. The parent node for the full dossier is [**https://osf.io/h7432/**](https://osf.io/h7432/){.uri}, and the table below summarises each component.

| Component | What | Outcome |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| `whp4b` | Original materials collected by COS | View-only |
| `cf8en` | **Author-provided code** – two Stata do-files (`eb_all.do`, `eb_ml_ESR.do`) supplied on request; data cannot be shared under GESIS terms (statement file `gxk9r`) | Code available; data restricted |
| `8fwrt` | Power analysis for the replication | – |
| `ezhcs` | **Push-button reproduction** (with author code) | **Failed** – file names in the code did not match the files available for download; 18 files referenced, 16 listed on the website |
| `4rjbf` | **Source-data reproduction** | **"Not reproduced"** – original effect size could not be extracted or re-calculated |
| `gr8u6` | **Multi100 robustness** – 5 independent reanalysts | All 5 coefficients negative (claim-consistent direction); partial r as recorded from −0.006 to −0.452 |
| `zt5y2` | **Secondary-data replication** (later Eurobarometer waves; preregistered) | **Not successful**. First report: b = +0.002, p = .046, N = 352,114; revised report of October 2026: b = +0.001, SE 0.0007, t = 1.428, p = 0.153, N = 331,668 |
| `6zqct` | Analyst's maintained fork (course fetch target) – holds the working materials and the data used in the course | <https://osf.io/6zqct/> |
| `8rtwe` | Official Multi100 archival record for analyst C6HJR | <https://osf.io/8rtwe/> |

The three activities reached three different verdicts on the same paper. Reproduction failed twice, in different ways. The robustness reanalysis held in sign, while its recorded effect sizes spanned two orders of magnitude, largely because of the way in which the test statistics were converted, and the replication on later waves was judged not successful. The glossary states that the three indicators are near-uncorrelated, and this case, documented entirely in public artefacts, shows what that means for a single paper. The [case study](cases/eu-frames/index.qmd) tells the story in full.

## Core readings

### The three *Nature* 2026 papers (SCORE)

- **Reproducibility:** @MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial – how often the central result of a paper can be recomputed from its own data. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10203-5>
- **Robustness:** @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness – Multi100, in which at least five analysts reanalysed each of a hundred claims. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09844-9>
- **Replicability:** @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial – how often claims hold on new data, under preregistered protocols. <https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-10078-y>
- @AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen – the SCORE programme, of which all three studies are part. <https://doi.org/10.31235/osf.io/46mnb>

### Vocabulary

- @NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms – a four-page glossary of the terms of repeatability; read it before the day. <https://doi.org/10.31222/osf.io/mqfp4_v1>
- @NosekErrington2020WhatReplication – what counts as a replication. <https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3000691>

### Estimands and analytical choices

- @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand – the steps from a theoretical estimand to an empirical one, and why a result means little until the estimand is stated. <https://doi.org/10.1177/00031224211004187>
- @SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne – the red-card study, in which twenty-nine teams analysed one dataset. <https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245917747646>
- @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial – the reanalysis of the red-card study that traced the spread of its results to teams answering different questions. <https://doi.org/10.1177/23780231211024421>

### Audit studies and the housing-audit case

- @Lipsky1980StreetLevelBureaucracy – the discretion of the officials who deliver public services in direct contact with citizens.
- @Pager2003MarkCriminalRecord and @BertrandMullainathan2004AreEmilyGreg – two field experiments on hiring that made the audit design familiar, the first with matched pairs of testers and the second with résumés that differed only in a name.
- @QuillianEtAl2017MetaanalysisFieldExperiments – a meta-analysis of field experiments on racial discrimination in hiring.
- @ButlerBroockman2011PoliticiansRaciallyDiscriminate and @WhiteEtAl2015WhatNeedVote – the audits of state legislators and local election officials on which the design of the OAs builds.
- @Gaddis2017HowBlackAre – how often the names used in audits are read as indicating the group that they are meant to indicate.
- @MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment – what conditioning on a variable that the treatment can change does to an experiment.
- @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias – the same problem in audit experiments that compare the content of replies, and the remedies, one of which analyst 25N5D chose.

### The multiverse and its critics

- @SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology and @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience – how undisclosed flexibility in analysis produces false positives, and the garden of forking paths.
- @SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse and @SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis – the multiverse analysis and the specification curve, the two proposals on which the curve of the claim draws.
- @DelGiudiceGangestad2021TravelersGuideMultiverse – a systematic framework for judging which analytic decisions are equivalent, and so which analyses belong in one multiverse.
- @BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers – a many-analysts study in which teams tested one hypothesis about immigration and social policy on the same data.
- @Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed – the case for a few thoughtful models over billions of regressions.
- @RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood and @LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne – what a multiverse is good for, and the argument that a fully specified question has only one correct analysis.
- @HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom – the multiverse as a teaching device.
- [Reading a specification curve](cases/eu-frames/reading-inference.qmd) – the course reading for the final part of the EU-frames day: why a large set of results is not a large set of independent tests, and what a single test across the whole curve can and cannot establish.

The [companion module on the multiverse](companion/multiverse.qmd) reads these against the curves of the claims.

### Preregistration

None of these is required, because everything is taught in the course, but they let you arrive with the ideas already in hand. All three are open access.

- Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven & Mellor (2018). The preregistration revolution. *PNAS*, 115(11), 2600–2606. <https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1708274114> – a short primer on the idea on which preregistration depends: predicting a result against explaining one after the fact, and the case, like ours, where the data already exist.
- The AsPredicted eight-question form – the short template on which the preregistration block of your report is modelled, listed on the OSF as the "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org". Live form: <https://aspredicted.org>; OSF listing: <https://help.osf.io/article/158-create-a-preregistration>.
- van den Akker, Weston, Campbell, et al. (2021). Preregistration of secondary data analysis: A template and tutorial. *Meta-Psychology*, 5, 2625. <https://doi.org/10.15626/MP.2020.2625> – the fuller template, built for our situation of reanalysing data that already exist, and the tool that a full version of the exercise would use.

## Companion curriculum

The modules of the [companion curriculum](companion/index.qmd) hold the teaching that a single day can only mention, each on a page of its own that stands without the others. The overview sets out the three strands into which they are grouped, which cases each module works on, and which tracks use it.

**Computational tools**

- [Getting started with R](companion/intro-r.qmd) – for participants arriving with no R at all, on the housing-audit data, with further sections on reading other formats, the grammar of graphics and the estimand habit; best read before the day.
- [Positron, RStudio and VS Code](companion/ide.qmd) – what an IDE does and what the course needs from one, with Positron pane by pane and RStudio and VS Code set beside it.
- [Quarto and reproducible documents](companion/quarto.qmd) – the format in which your report and every page of this site are written.

**Data management and sharing**

- [Social science data sources](companion/data-sources.qmd) – a map of the survey programmes, archives, panels and official statistics, with the access rule for each, and a screen-by-screen walk through the GESIS download of the EU-frames case.
- [Building the analysis file](companion/data-management.qmd) – the two workspace scripts of the EU-frames case that turn your own sixteen GESIS downloads into the respondent file and then into the panel.
- [Reproducibility repositories](companion/repositories.qmd) – research-data archives, the public records behind the housing-audit and EU-frames cases, and preregistration templates in more depth.
- [Git and GitHub](companion/git-github.qmd) – version control and publishing your own report, kept out of the core day so that it can be learned separately.

**Statistical methods**

- [Audit experiments](companion/experiments.qmd) – field experiments on discrimination, on the housing-audit case: random assignment, names as treatments, comparisons among replies, randomisation inference, power and the ethics of deception.
- [Binary outcomes](companion/binary-outcomes.qmd) – proportions, linear probability models and logistic regression on the housing-audit case, and a yes-or-no survey item in clustered data on the EU-frames case.
- [Causal graphs & adjustment sets](companion/dags.qmd) – confounders, mediators and colliders, conditioning on a reply in the housing-audit case, and confounding by country in the EU-frames panel.
- [The items behind the scales](companion/measurement.qmd), [Weights](companion/weighting.qmd) and [Missing answers](companion/missingness.qmd) – how the scales of the EU-frames and immigration-and-trust cases are built from the items of the surveys, the three kinds of weight, and the respondents who mention nothing.
- [Event-history analysis](companion/event-history.qmd) – censoring, the life table, person-period data and the discrete-time models of two competing ways out of a union, on the cohabitation case.
- [The statistical methods behind the course](companion/stats-methods.qmd) – every model fitted on the data of the EU-frames case, from a first `lm()` through fixed and random effects to multilevel, Bayesian and ordered-beta models.
- [The individual level](companion/individual-level.qmd) and [Simulation as a method](companion/simulation.qmd) – the published specification of the EU-frames case at the level of respondents, on a validated simulated twin, and simulation as a way of checking a method.
- [The multiverse and its critics](companion/multiverse.qmd) – where specification curves came from, the purposes that they serve, the current debate about them, and the curves of the housing-audit and EU-frames cases.

## If you are at Newcastle University
